newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli leader criticised for tension with Syria.
newsitem.headline: Israeli leader criticised for tension with Syria.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is under fire from critics who say he is to blame for statements that have prompted Syrian troop movements now worrying Israelis.
Syrian President Hafez al-Assad's redeployment of up to a third of his 35,000 troops in Lebanon has given Israelis a case of war jitters.
Some of the Syrian soldiers are within striking distance of a key Israeli position on the Golan Heights.
Israeli opposition leaders and Egypt's ambassador to Israel said combative remarks by leaders of Netanyahu's three-month-old government were largely to blame.
On Monday, Ehud Barak, a former army chief and aspiring leader of the opposition Labour party, demanded Netanyahu "control his tongue".
On Tuesday, Egyptian Ambassador Mohammad Bassiouny said statements threatening to the Syrians had led to a swift escalation.
"From the beginning there were some statements which caused this tensions. These troops are not making tension. This is a defensive position," Bassiouny told Israel Radio.
Last month, Netanyahu warned of an escalation if Israelis and their militia allies came under further attack from Hizbollah guerrillas, who are supplied through Syria.
At the time he threatened Israel would not "stand still".
Israeli officials have since tried to ease tensions. On Tuesday Netanyahu had an hour-long private meeting with Labour leader Shimon Peres, the man he ousted in May.
But when he was asked about opposition claims that his tough talk had exacerbated matters, Netanyahu told reporters: "That's irresponsible and not true.
"We've been very careful, very prudent and what Syria is trying to do is evidently to put psychological pressure on Israel and on this new government. It's not going to work."
The prime minister and his defence chief assured Israelis that events in the north were being closely monitored and that Israel was prepared for anything.
U.S. Ambassador to Beirut, Richard Jones, on Tuesday described the Syrian troop redeployment as "not alarming", saying fears of a military confrontation were "far-fetched".
Netanyahu opposed Peres's policy of trading occupied Arab land for peace and says the Golan, captured from Syria in the 1967 Middle East war, must remain under Israeli sovereignty.
Syria wants Israel to return all of the strategic plateau.
Ze'ev Maoz, head of the Tel Aviv University Jaffee Centre for Strategic Studies, said Syria's moves were prompted both by the statements and by the policies of the right-wing government.
"(It) is clearly a signal to Israel that lack of progress on negotiations with Syria is a dangerous situation in that it destabilises the relations," he told Israel Radio.
Netanyahu and the United States have been trying to come up with a formula to restart negotiations severed by Israel after Moslem suicide bombings in February and March.
U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross, in the region this week, has been trying to revive negotiations also between Israel and the Palestinians.
Ross and Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai were due to meet Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in separate meetings on Wednesday in the self-ruled Gaza Strip.
